original_value: This study examines the reasons why authors publish in ‘predatory’OAjournals. In total, 50 journals were randomly selected from Beall's list of ‘predatory’ journals. Different methods, includingWHOIStracking, were utilized to query basic information about the selected journals, including location and registrant. Then, 300 articles were randomly selected from within selected journals in various scientific fields. Authors of the selected articles were contacted and sent survey questions to complete. A grounded theory qualitative methods approach was used for data collection and analysis. The results demonstrated that most of these journals were located in the developing world, usually Asia or Africa, even when they claimed they were in theUSAorUK. Furthermore, four themes emerged after authors’ survey responses were coded, categorized, and sub‐categorized. The themes were:social identity threat, unawareness, high pressure,andlack of research proficiency. Scholars in the developing world felt that reputable Western journals might be prejudiced against them and sometimes felt more comfortable publishing in journals from the developing world. Other scholars were unaware of the reputation of the journals in which they published and would not have selected them had they known. However, some scholars said they would still have published in the same journals if their institution recognised them. The pressure to ‘publish or perish’ was another factor influencing many scholars’ decisions to publish in these fast‐turnaround journals. In some cases, researchers did not have adequate guidance and felt they lacked the knowledge of research to submit to a more reputable journal. More needs to be done by institutions and reputable journals to make researchers aware of the problem of ‘predatory’ journals.

result.paraphrase: This study investigates why authors choose to publish in predatory OA journals. Fifty journals were randomly chosen from Beall's list of predatory journals, and WHOIS tracking and other methods were used to gather basic details such as location and registrant. The researchers then randomly selected 300 articles from those journals across different scientific fields and contacted the authors with survey questions. Data collection and analysis followed a grounded theory qualitative approach. The findings showed that most of the journals were based in the developing world, typically Asia or Africa, even though they claimed to be in the USA or UK. After the survey responses were coded, categorized, and subcategorized, four themes emerged: social identity threat, unawareness, high pressure, and lack of research proficiency. Scholars in the developing world felt reputable Western journals might be biased against them and sometimes preferred journals from the developing world. Others were unaware of the journals’ reputations and said they would not have chosen them had they known. Some said they would still have published in the same journals if their institution recognized them. Pressure to publish or perish also influenced many decisions to use these fast-turnaround journals. In some cases, researchers lacked sufficient guidance and felt they did not know enough about research to submit to a more reputable journal. Institutions and reputable journals need to do more to alert researchers to the problem of predatory journals.
